Les hommes ont mangé (sujet transitif pl: The men ate (transitive plural subject): Gizon___ jan dute
Je l'ai dit aux amis : lagun___ esan die: I told my friends: lagun___ esan diet
Indéfini, défini et partitif en usage: Indefinite, definite and partitive in use
Le nom défini (etxea) désigne quelque ch: The definite noun (etxea) refers to something specific; the indefinite bat introduces a new element; the partitive (-rik) replaces the indefinite in negative or interrogative sentences. For a general object, the definite is often used.
Au restaurant on demande souvent ... bat: In a restaurant you often ask for ... bat (kafe bat, mesedez).
bat follows the bare noun: kafe bat.
Le basque n'a ni masculin ni féminin. hu: Basque has neither masculine nor feminine. hura means he, she or it, and adjectives don't agree in gender. Sex is specified with separate words: gizon (man) and emakume (woman).
-a final dans neska ou ama n'est pas une: The final -a in neska or ama is not a feminine marker.
Comment dit-on « elle est venue » ?: How do you say « she came »?
Hura vaut aussi bien pour il que pour el: Hura works for both he and she; izan is the auxiliary of etorri.
Termes de parenté selon le sexe du locut: Kinship terms depending on the speaker's sex
Plusieurs mots de parenté changent selon: Several kinship words change depending on the sex of the speaker: brother is anaia for a man and neba for a woman; sister is arreba for a man and ahizpa for a woman.
Piège : cette distinction n'existe pas e: Trap: this distinction doesn't exist in French.
Une femme parle de son frère. Quel mot e: A woman is talking about her brother. Which word does she use?
Neba est le frère d'une femme ; anaia le: Neba is a woman's brother; anaia is a man's brother.
Pour tout, tous, on utilise guztia/guzti: For all, every, use guztia/guztiak or dena/denak after the noun. The noun is then indefinite and the quantifier carries the article and the cases.
Asko (beaucoup) reste invariable ; guzti: Asko (a lot) stays invariable; guztiak changes.
Le quantificateur suit le nom nu et pren: The quantifier follows the bare noun and takes -ak: etxe guztiak.
De 1 à 10 : bat, bi, hiru, lau, bost, se: From 1 to 10: bat, bi, hiru, lau, bost, sei, zazpi, zortzi, bederatzi, hamar. Numbers 12 to 17 are formed with hama- (hamabi, hamahiru, hamalau, hamabost, hamasei, hamazazpi). Three forms are irregular: 11 = hamaika, 18 = hemezortzi and 19 = hemeretzi. 20 = hogei.
hamaika s'emploie aussi pour une grande: hamaika is also used for a large quantity (hamaika gauza = a thousand things).
Le basque compte par vingtaines : 20 hog: Basque counts in twenties: 20 hogei, 40 berrogei (2 x 20), 60 hirurogei (3 x 20), 80 laurogei (4 x 20). The tens in between are made with hamar: 30 hogeita hamar, 50 berrogeita hamar, 70 hirurogeita hamar, 90 laurogeita hamar.
Pour 80 le basque dit quatre-vingts : la: For 80 Basque says four twenties: laurogei, and for 90 four twenties and ten.
Les nombres entre les vingtaines se form: Numbers between the twenties are formed with the twenty + ta/eta + unit: hogei + eta becomes hogeita. They are written as two words: hogeita bat, hogeita bi, berrogeita bost.
Après hogeita on emploie le nombre norma: After hogeita you use the normal number: hogeita hamabi = 32.
100 = ehun ; les centaines sont ehun ave: 100 = ehun; the hundreds are ehun with the multiplier attached: berrehun (200), hirurehun (300), laurehun (400), bostehun (500), seiehun (600), zazpiehun (700), zortziehun (800), bederatziehun (900). 1000 = mila. The unit follows with eta.
1995 se dit mila bederatziehun eta lauro: 1995 is said mila bederatziehun eta laurogeita hamabost.
500 is written as one word: bostehun.
Les ordinaux se forment avec -garren (sa: Ordinals are formed with -garren (except lehen/lehenengo for first and azken for last). They come before the noun: bigarren, hirugarren, laugarren, bosgarren, seigarren...
Le nom suit l'ordinal : hirugarren solai: The noun follows the ordinal: hirugarren solairuan bizi naiz = I live on the third floor.
Pour 1 h on dit ordu bata da ; pour les: For 1 o'clock you say ordu bata da; for the other hours, the number takes the plural article and the verb is dira: biak, hirurak, laurak, bostak, seiak, zazpiak... Quarter past is eta laurden, half past eta erdiak, quarter to laurden gutxi.
Une heure se dit da (singulier), les aut: One o'clock uses da (singular), the other hours use dira.
Les heures à partir de deux : chiffre +: Hours from two on: number + -ak + dira.
One o'clock is singular: ordu bata da.
Pour dire à (telle heure), on met le chi: To say at (a given time), put the number in the plural locative: bietan (2:00), hiruretan (3:00), lauretan (4:00), bostetan (5:00), seietan (6:00), zazpietan (7:00), zortzietan (8:00), bederatzietan (9:00), hamarretan (10:00), hamaiketan (11:00), hamabietan (12:00). For 1:00: ordu batean.
nous sortirons à cinq heures: we'll go out at five o'clock
je déjeune à une heure: I have lunch at one o'clock
Ne pas confondre avec zortziak dira (il: Don't confuse with zortziak dira (it's eight o'clock).
La date se construit en ordre inverse du: The date is built in the reverse order from French: year + -ko, month + -(r)en, day + -a. The month is in the genitive. To say on (the day), the day takes -ean: urriaren 1ean. Months and days are written in lowercase.
The order is year, month, day.
L'ordre basque : année + ko, mois + ren,: The Basque order: year + ko, month + ren, day + a.
Pour le jour précis on emploie -ean : ma: For the exact day you use -ean: martxoaren 15ean.
Jours : astelehena, asteartea, asteazken: Days: astelehena, asteartea, asteazkena, osteguna, ostirala, larunbata, igandea. Months: urtarrila, otsaila, martxoa, apirila, maiatza, ekaina, uztaila, abuztua, iraila, urria, azaroa, abendua. To say on Monday: astelehenean; every Monday: astelehenetan.
La semaine commence le lundi : astelehen: The week starts on Monday: astelehen is the first day.
On dit ostiralean pour le (jour) et osti: You say ostiralean for on (the day) and ostiraletan for every Friday.
Âge et durée : ukan avec urte: Age and duration: ukan with urte
Pour l'âge on emploie le verbe avoir (uk: For age you use the verb to have (ukan) and the plural: Hogeita bost urte ditut = I'm 25 years old. You don't say to be (izan).
L'auxiliaire est au pluriel (ditut) car: The auxiliary is plural (ditut) because urte is a plural object.
J'ai 30 ans : Hogeita hamar urte ___: I'm 30 years old: Hogeita hamar urte ___
Pour l'âge on emploie dituzu/ditut (plur: For age you use dituzu/ditut (plural object), not izan.
La moitié se dit erdi (placé après le no: Half is erdi (placed after the noun), a quarter laurden, a third heren. For shopping: kilo erdi (500 g), litro erdi (half a liter). Percentage is expressed with ehuneko or %.
un demi-kilo de fromage, s'il vous plaît: half a kilo of cheese, please
erdi se place après le nom : kilo erdi,: erdi goes after the noun: kilo erdi, never erdi kilo.
erdi follows the noun: kilo erdi.
Pour demander le prix, on dit Zenbat da?: To ask the price, say Zenbat da? (how much is it?) or Zenbat balio du? (how much does it cost?). You answer with the number + euro: Bost euro da. The noun euro stays invariable after a number.
You say bi euro (never bi euroak).
Après un nombre le nom reste invariable: After a number the noun stays invariable: bost euro.
Nor / nork : le sujet change de cas: Nor / nork: the subject changes case
Avec un verbe intransitif (aller, venir,: With an intransitive verb (go, come, be), the subject is in the absolutive: ni, zu, Mikel. With a transitive verb, the subject is in the ergative: nik, zuk, Mikelek, and the object is in the absolutive. So you must say nik with ikusi (to see) but ni with joan (to go).
Erreur fréquente : dire Ni ikusi dut au: Common mistake: saying Ni ikusi dut instead of Nik ikusi dut.
___ liburua irakurri dut. (Moi, j'ai lu: ___ liburua irakurri dut. (I read the book)
Sujet d'un verbe transitif : ergatif nik: Subject of a transitive verb: ergative nik.
Sujet d'un verbe intransitif : absolutif: Subject of an intransitive verb: absolutive ni.
L'auxiliaire des verbes intransitifs est: The auxiliary of intransitive verbs is izan. Present: naiz, zara, da, gara, zarete, dira. Past: nintzen, zinen, zen, ginen, zineten, ziren. It agrees with the subject.
izan est aussi le verbe être : Euskaldun: izan is also the verb to be: Euskalduna naiz = I'm a Basque speaker.
izan à la 1re personne du pluriel : gara: izan in the 1st person plural: gara.
Past of izan in the 3rd person plural: ziren.
Les verbes transitifs prennent l'auxilia: Transitive verbs take the auxiliary ukan (form *edun). Present: dut, duzu, du, dugu, duzue, dute. Past: nuen, zenuen, zuen, genuen, zenuten, zuten. The marked person is the ergative one (the subject).
*edun est la forme théorique du verbe (i: *edun is the theoretical form of the verb (infinitive); only its conjugated forms are used.
Tu as lu le livre : liburua irakurri ___: You read the book: liburua irakurri ___
L'auxiliaire s'accorde avec l'objet plur: The auxiliary agrees with the plural object
Avec un objet pluriel, l'auxiliaire pren: With a plural object, the auxiliary takes the plural form: dut becomes ditut, duzu dituzu, du ditu, dugu ditugu, duzue dituzue, dute dituzte. Past: nituen, zenituen, zituen...
L'objet pluriel entraîne aussi bi + nom: A plural object also goes with bi + noun (bi liburu irakurri ditut).
J'ai lu les livres : liburuak irakurri _: I read the books: liburuak irakurri ___
The object liburuak is plural: ditut.
J'ai acheté deux livres : bi liburu eros: I bought two books: bi liburu erosi ___
Avec un nombre, l'objet est pluriel : di: With a number, the object is plural: ditut.
L'auxiliaire contient aussi l'objet quan: The auxiliary also contains the object when it is me, you, us. Common forms: zaitut (I ... you), nauzu (you ... me), du (he/she ... it), nau (he/she ... me), gaitu (he/she ... us).
Nik ez zaitut ulertzen = je ne te compre: Nik ez zaitut ulertzen = I don't understand you.
NOR-NORI : gustatu et verbes à datif: NOR-NORI: gustatu and verbs with a dative
Certains verbes demandent un datif : gus: Some verbs require a dative: gustatu (to like), iruditu (to seem), falta izan (to be missing). The auxiliary is izan with the forms zait, zaio, zaie...; if the subject is plural: zaizkit, zaizkio. The person who likes is in the dative.
Le sujet (ce qu'on aime) est l'absolutif: The subject (what is liked) is in the absolutive: kafea gustatzen zait = I like coffee (lit. coffee is pleasing to me).
J'aime le café : Niri kafea gustatzen __: I like coffee: Niri kafea gustatzen ___
J'aime les livres (sujet pluriel) : Niri: I like books (plural subject): Niri liburuak gustatzen ___
Quand il y a trois éléments (sujet, obje: When there are three elements (subject, object, recipient), the auxiliary contains all of them. Me to him/her: diot; me to you: dizut; him/her to me: dit; him/her to them: die; me to them: diet. Plural object: dizkiot, dizkizut...
À ne pas confondre : dio (lui, à lui) et: Don't confuse: dio (to him/her) and die (to them).
Je t'ai donné le livre : Liburua eman __: I gave you the book: Liburua eman ___
Me to you, one object: dizut.
Il leur a donné le livre : Liburua eman: He/she gave them the book: Liburua eman ___
Verbes nominaux avec egin : toujours uka: Nominal verbs with egin: always ukan
Les verbes formés avec egin (faire) comm: Verbs formed with egin (to do) such as lan egin, hitz egin, lo egin, barre egin, negar egin take the auxiliary ukan, even if they correspond to an intransitive verb in French. The nominal object stays without an article.
Négation : Ez dut lorik egin = je n'ai p: Negation: Ez dut lorik egin = I didn't sleep.
J'ai travaillé hier : Atzo lan egin ___: I worked yesterday: Atzo lan egin ___
Pour la faim, la soif, la peur, on emplo: For hunger, thirst, fear, use izan: gose naiz, egarri naiz, beldur naiz. For heat, cold, pain, use ukan: hotz dut, bero dut, buruko mina dut. For the weather: euria ari du.
Ne pas dire hotz naiz : cela signifierai: Don't say hotz naiz: it would mean I am cold (by nature).
Pour le froid on emploie ukan : hotz dut: For cold you use ukan: hotz dut.
Pour la faim on emploie izan : gose naiz: For hunger you use izan: gose naiz.
Verbes intransitifs inattendus : jaio, h: Unexpected intransitive verbs: jaio, hil, bizi
Les verbes jaio (naître), hil (mourir) e: The verbs jaio (to be born), hil (to die) and bizi (to live) are intransitive and take izan. But hil in the sense of to kill is transitive: Mikelek zakurra hil du.
Même verbe, deux auxiliaires : hil da (e: Same verb, two auxiliaries: hil da (died) / hil du (killed).
Verbes modaux : behar et nahi avec ukan: Modal verbs: behar and nahi with ukan
Avec behar (devoir) et nahi (vouloir), l: With behar (must) and nahi (to want), the auxiliary is ukan (dut, duzu...) even if the main verb is intransitive. For ezin (cannot) you use the auxiliary of the main verb: ezin dut ulertu.
Erreur fréquente : joan behar naiz (faux: Common mistake: joan behar naiz (wrong) instead of joan behar dut.
Je dois partir (joan) : Joan behar ___: I have to leave (joan): Joan behar ___
Le basque a un tutoiement intime, le hit: Basque has an intimate form of address, the hitano or hika, with the pronoun hi. It distinguishes between men (-k) and women (-n): Zer egiten duk? (man) / Zer egiten dun? (woman). It is used in the family and among close friends, mostly outside written batua. The standard usage is zu.
que fais-tu ? (à un homme): what are you doing? (to a man)
que fais-tu ? (à une femme): what are you doing? (to a woman)
Un apprenant doit utiliser zu ; le hitan: A learner should use zu; hitano can be understood without having to be produced.
Quel est le pronom familier du hitano ?: What is the informal pronoun of hitano?
Hi est le pronom intime ; zu est le pron: Hi is the intimate pronoun; zu is the standard pronoun.
egon exprime le lieu et l'état temporair: egon expresses place and temporary state. Present: nago, zaude, dago, gaude, zaudete, daude. Past: nengoen, zeunden, zegoen, geunden, zeundeten, zeuden. The verb izan is used for identity (euskalduna naiz).
egon ne s'utilise pas pour la profession: egon is not used for profession: irakaslea naiz = I'm a teacher.
Verbe de mouvement synthétique. Présent: Synthetic motion verb. Present: noa, zoaz, doa, goaz, zoazte, doaz. Past: nindoan, zindoazen, zihoan, gindoazen, zindoazten, zihoazen. The participle is joan (joan naiz = I went).
La forme goaz signifie nous allons ; Goa: The form goaz means we are going; Goazen! is the exhortation (let's go).
Présent : nator, zatoz, dator, gatoz, za: Present: nator, zatoz, dator, gatoz, zatozte, datoz. Past: nentorren, zentozen, zetorren, gentozen, zentozten, zetozen. The participle is etorri (etorri naiz = I came). The imperative is zatoz (come).
etorri indique un mouvement vers le locu: etorri indicates movement toward the speaker; joan movement away.
Le bus arrive (vers nous) : Autobusa ___: The bus is coming (toward us): Autobusa ___
The imperative of etorri for tu is zatoz.
ibili : marcher, être en mouvement: ibili: to walk, to be on the move
Verbe synthétique de mouvement (se prome: Synthetic motion verb (to walk around, to work/function, to be active). Present: nabil, zabiltza, dabil, gabiltza, zabiltzate, dabiltza. Participle: ibili. Don't confuse it with joan (to go).
Mikel est en montagne à marcher: Mikel is out walking in the mountains
ibili suppose un mouvement continu ou ré: ibili implies continuous or repeated movement.
Je me promène dans la rue : Kalean ___: I'm walking down the street: Kalean ___
eduki signifie avoir ou tenir. Présent :: eduki means to have or to hold. Present: daukat, daukazu, dauka, daukagu, daukazue, daukate. With a plural object: dauzkat, dauzkazu, dauzka, dauzkagu, dauzkazue, dauzkate. It is more concrete than ukan.
Le sens abstrait avoir (j'ai lu) se dit: The abstract sense of to have (I have read) is expressed with the auxiliary dut, not with daukat.
J'ai deux frères : Bi anaia ___: I have two brothers: Bi anaia ___
J'ai une maison (avec eduki) : Etxe bat: I have a house (with eduki): Etxe bat ___
jakin signifie savoir (un fait, une lang: jakin means to know (a fact, a language); ezagutu means to know (a person, a place). Present of jakin: dakit, dakizu, daki, dakigu, dakizue, dakite. Future of to know: jakingo.
Ne pas dire Mikel dakit pour je connais: Don't say Mikel dakit for I know Mikel: you need ezagutzen dut.
For a person, you use ezagutu.
La forme synthétique de jakin au présent: The synthetic form of jakin in the present: dakit.
ekarri et eraman : apporter / emporter: ekarri and eraman: to bring / to take away
ekarri signifie apporter (vers ici), era: ekarri means to bring (toward here), eraman means to take away (away from here). Presents: dakart, dakarzu, dakar... and daramat, daramazu, darama... With a plural object: dakartzat... / daramatzat...
je t'apporterai le livre demain: I'll bring you the book tomorrow
La distinction ici/là-bas est obligatoir: The here/there distinction is mandatory in Basque.
J'emporte le livre (loin d'ici) :: I'm taking the book (away from here):
L'habituel se forme à partir du particip: The habitual is formed from the participle: -tu becomes -tzen (hartu: hartzen); -n is replaced by -ten (esan: esaten, jan: jaten); -i drops and -ten is added, or -tzen after l, n, r (ikasi: ikasten, etorri: etortzen, ibili: ibiltzen). A few forms are irregular.
ikasi donne ikasten ; ezagutu donne ezag: ikasi gives ikasten; ezagutu gives ezagutzen.
Le futur s'obtient avec -ko après voyell: The future is formed with -ko after a vowel and -go after -n. It is followed by the auxiliary. izan gives izango, egon egongo, egin egingo.
Futur de venir : bihar etorriko naiz = j: Future of to come: bihar etorriko naiz = I will come tomorrow.
Le participe de izan est izan ; celui de: The participle of izan is izan; that of ukan is also izan: izan naiz (I have been) and izan dut (I have had); only the auxiliary changes. egon naiz means I have been (somewhere). In the future: izango naiz (I will be) and izango dut (I will have).
L'auxiliaire permet de distinguer les de: The auxiliary makes it possible to tell the two meanings of izan apart.
J'ai eu une maison (ukan) : Etxe bat iza: I had a house (ukan): Etxe bat izan ___
izan comme participe de ukan, auxiliaire: izan as the participle of ukan, auxiliary dut.
Habituel et progressif : -ten et ari iza: Habitual and progressive: -ten and ari izan
Le participe en -ten/-tzen + auxiliaire: The participle in -ten/-tzen + auxiliary expresses habit or the general present. For an action in progress, use ari izan: participle in -ten + ari naiz/zara/da. In the past: ari nintzen, ari zen...
que fais-tu en ce moment ?: what are you doing right now?
il/elle parlait au téléphone: he/she was talking on the phone
Euskaraz hitz egiten dut = je parle (d'h: Euskaraz hitz egiten dut = I speak (habitually); Euskaraz hitz egiten ari naiz = I'm speaking (right now).
Le parfait (participe + présent de l'aux: The present perfect (participle + present of the auxiliary) expresses a completed action that is recent or still relevant; the preterite (participle + past of the auxiliary) expresses a distant past action. izan: naiz / nintzen; ukan: dut / nuen.
la semaine dernière je suis allé à Bilba: last week I went to Bilbao
Le prétérit s'emploie avec une marque de: The preterite is used with a past time marker: atzo, joan den astean, iaz.
Quelle forme est le prétérit (passé) de: Which form is the preterite (past) of ukan in the 1st person singular?
Le prétérit de ukan (1re personne) est n: The preterite of ukan (1st person) is nuen; dut is the present, nintzen the preterite of izan.
Pour une habitude passée (je faisais sou: For a past habit (I often used to), use the participle in -ten + the past auxiliary. This corresponds to the English "used to" + verb.
petit, le dimanche j'allais à la montagn: as a child, on Sundays I used to go to the mountains
je buvais du café chaque jour: I used to drink coffee every day
ma mère faisait du pain: my mother used to make bread
Pour une action ponctuelle on utilise jo: For a one-off action use joan nintzen; for a habit joaten nintzen.
J'allais (habituellement) au marché : Az: I used to go (habitually) to the market: Azokara ___ nintzen
Le conditionnel se forme avec le futur -: The conditional is formed with the future -ko + the conditional auxiliary. For ukan: nuke, zenuke, luke, genuke, zenukete, lukete. For izan: nintzateke, zinateke, litzateke, ginateke, zinatekete, lirateke. Nahi nuke is the polite form for I would like.
Au restaurant et en boutique, nahi nuke: In restaurants and shops, nahi nuke is more polite than nahi dut.
Je voudrais un café : Kafe bat nahi ___: I'd like a coffee: Kafe bat nahi ___
La condition réelle se marque par ba- co: The real condition is marked by ba- attached to the conjugated auxiliary: ba + du = badu, ba + dugu = badugu, ba + zara = bazara. The unreal condition uses ba- + the hypothetical auxiliary: banu, bazenu, balitz...
s'il pleut, je resterai à la maison: if it rains, I'll stay at home
si tu as besoin de quelque chose, dis-le: if you need something, say so
si tu viens, je te le dirai: if you come, I'll tell you
si j'avais de l'argent, j'achèterais une: if I had money, I would buy a house
Le ba- est collé au verbe conjugué, il n: The ba- is attached to the conjugated verb; it is not placed at the front of the sentence.
L'impératif se forme avec des formes syn: The imperative is formed with synthetic or periphrastic forms. For you come: zatoz; for you go: zoaz; for you stay: zaude. For a transitive verb, use participle + ezazu: hartu ezazu, egin ezazu, eman iezadazu. The prohibition is made with ez + participle: ez ukitu.
donne-moi un pain, s'il te plaît: give me a loaf of bread, please
Pour s'adresser à plusieurs : zatozte, z: To address several people: zatozte, zoazte, zaudete.
joan gives zoaz in the imperative.
Le subjonctif s'emploie surtout après na: The subjunctive is used mainly after nahi izan (to want someone to ...): reduced participle + subjunctive form + -n. For zu: zaitezen; for hura (intransitive): dadin; for hura (transitive): dezan. You can also say more simply Zuk etortzea nahi dut.
je veux que tu viennes (forme nominalisé: I want you to come (nominalized form)
La forme nominalisée en -tzea (Zuk etort: The nominalized form in -tzea (Zuk etortzea nahi dut) is a common alternative.
Je veux que tu viennes : Etor ___ nahi d: I want you to come: Etor ___ nahi dut
Subjonctif de izan à la 2e personne + n: Subjunctive of izan in the 2nd person + n: zaitezen.
Pouvoir : dezaket et ezin: Being able to: dezaket and ezin
Pour pouvoir, on emploie la forme potent: To express can, use the synthetic potential form with a transitive verb: dezaket, dezakezu, dezake, dezakegu, dezakezue, dezakete. The verb is reduced to its stem (ikus, edan, jan). The negation is made with ezin dut + participle.
Le verbe se met au radical : ikus dezake: The verb goes in its stem form: ikus dezaket (not ikusi dezaket).
La négation ez se place juste avant l'au: The negation ez goes right before the auxiliary, which precedes the participle: ez + aux + participle. Synthetic verbs are also negated with ez before the form: ez dakit, ez noa. Negative words (ezer, inor, inon, inoiz) are added to ez and placed near the verb (ez dut ezer ikusi).
En français on dit je n'ai pas vu ; en b: In French you say je n'ai pas vu; in Basque the order is ez dut ikusi (never ikusi ez dut).
La forme synthétique se nie par ez devan: The synthetic form is negated by ez before it: ez dakit.
L'ordre de base est sujet (ergatif) + ob: The basic order is subject (ergative) + object + participle + auxiliary. The conjugated verb comes at the end. In the negative, ez + auxiliary precedes the participle: Mikelek ez du liburua irakurri.
French is SVO; Basque is SOV.
Dans une phrase neutre, où se place l'au: In a neutral sentence, where does the auxiliary (du, dut...) go?
L'ordre de base est SOV : sujet, objet,: The basic order is SOV: subject, object, participle, auxiliary (Mikelek liburua irakurtzen du).
Focalisation : l'élément mis en relief a: Focus: the highlighted element before the verb
L'élément mis en relief se place juste d: The highlighted element goes right in front of the verb. Question words (zer, nor, non...) are always there. To stress the subject, move it in front of the verb phrase.
c'est Mikel qui lit le livre: it's Mikel who reads the book
La question zer nahi duzu? met zer devan: The question zer nahi duzu? puts zer in front of the auxiliary.
Le mot interrogatif se place juste avant: The question word goes right before the verb.
Pour une question fermée, on place al ju: For a closed question, put al right before the auxiliary; you can also keep the declarative order with rising intonation. al is written separately.
Réponses : Bai (oui) / Ez (non). On répo: Answers: Bai (yes) / Ez (no). You often answer with the verb: Bai, hitz egiten dut.
Parlez-vous basque ? Euskaraz hitz egite: Do you speak Basque? Euskaraz hitz egiten ___ duzu?
zer = quoi ; nor = qui ; noiz = quand ;: zer = what; nor = who; noiz = when; non = where; nora = where to; nondik = where from; nola = how; zergatik = why; zenbat = how much; zein = which; nongoa = where from (origin). The words follow the cases: nork (ergative), nori (dative), norekin (with whom).
Pour qui est sujet d'un verbe transitif,: For who as the subject of a transitive verb, say nork.
Où habites-tu ? ___ bizi zara?: Where do you live? ___ bizi zara?
Pourquoi n'es-tu pas venu ? ___ ez zara: Why didn't you come? ___ ez zara etorri?
Après dire, penser, savoir (affirmation): After to say, to think, to know (affirmation), the subordinate clause takes -(e)la attached to the auxiliary: dela, zela, dutela. For an indirect question (if, which, who), use -(e)n: den, duen.
je ne sais pas si Mikel est venu: I don't know if Mikel came
Il a dit que Mikel est venu : Mikel etor: He said that Mikel came: Mikel etorri ___ esan du
La proposition relative précède son nom: The relative clause comes before its noun and ends with the suffix -(e)n on the auxiliary. The noun follows the auxiliary in -n. French puts the relative clause after the noun: it's the opposite.
un ami qui vit à Saint-Sébastien: a friend who lives in San Sebastian
Ordre : relative + nom : irakurri dudan: Order: relative clause + noun: irakurri dudan liburua, not liburua irakurri dudan.
The relative clause comes before the noun.
-(e)nean signifie quand (en répétition o: -(e)nean means when (for repeated events or at a given moment). It attaches to the conjugated auxiliary: naizenean, zarenean, denean (present), nintzenean, zenean (past). The non-finite form -tzean/-tean simply marks at the time of.
quand j'arrive à la maison, je dîne: when I get home, I have dinner
quand je suis arrivé à la maison, il/ell: when I got home, he/she was asleep
quand Mikel est venu, nous avons dîné: when Mikel came, we had dinner
en arrivant à la maison, je t'appellerai: when I get home, I'll call you
Passé : -nean avec l'auxiliaire au passé: Past: -nean with the auxiliary in the past (nintzenean).
Parce que : -(e)lako collé à l'auxiliair: Because: -(e)lako attached to the auxiliary (dut -> dudalako). Since: -(e)nez gero. In formal style: zeren + bait- on the auxiliary.
je ne sortirai pas parce que je suis fat: I won't go out because I'm tired
puisque il pleut, je resterai à la maiso: since it's raining, I'll stay at home
je ne suis pas allé parce que j'étais fa: I didn't go because I was tired
je ne suis pas sorti parce qu'il pleuvai: I didn't go out because it was raining
-lako is used in everyday speech; zeren ... bait- is more of a written form.
Avec ez, on utilise les mots négatifs ez: With ez, use the negative words ezer (nothing), inor (nobody), inon (nowhere), inoiz (never). The indefinite object takes the partitive -(r)ik: Ez dut dirurik. For me neither: nik ere ez.
En basque on garde ez : la double négati: In Basque you keep ez: the double negation is normal.
Je n'ai rien vu : Ez dut ___ ikusi: I didn't see anything: Ez dut ___ ikusi
ezer s'emploie avec ez devant l'auxiliai: ezer is used with ez in front of the auxiliary.
ere (aussi) suit le mot : Nik ere. baina: ere (also) follows the word: Nik ere. baina (but) opens the clause. ordea (however) goes after the first word. baino means than in a comparison: the term of comparison comes before baino.
ere ne ouvre jamais la phrase ; ordea n': ere never opens the sentence; ordea never opens the sentence either.
Moi aussi je parle basque : ___ ere eusk: I speak Basque too: ___ ere euskaraz hitz egiten dut
Sujet d'un verbe transitif : ergatif nik: Subject of a transitive verb: ergative nik ere.
Le basque emploie des postpositions : le: Basque uses postpositions: the noun in the genitive is followed by a locative word (gainean, azpian, aurrean, atzean, ondoan, barruan, kanpoan). For pronouns: nire ondoan.
Ordre inverse du français : la table + s: Reverse order from French: the table + on, not on the table.
Le suffixe -garri forme un adjectif au s: The suffix -garri forms an adjective meaning causing, worthy of. It attaches to the stem of a verb or a noun, sometimes with an adjustment: harritu gives harrigarri.
-kor forme un adjectif qui exprime la te: -kor forms an adjective that expresses tendency or disposition. It is found with simple words such as bai and ez.
baikor vient de bai (oui) et ezkor de ez: baikor comes from bai (yes) and ezkor from ez (no).
-tasun transforme un adjectif ou un nom: -tasun turns an adjective or a noun into an abstract noun (quality, state). It corresponds to the English -ity, -ness, -ship.
Comparez le français : liberté, égalité,: Compare in English: liberty, equality, solidarity.
-tza forme un nom d'action ou d'état à p: -tza forms a noun of action or state from a verb; -kuntza forms nouns for collective activities or fields. These are the endings of common abstract nouns.
Ne confondez pas hizkuntza (langue en gé: Don't confuse hizkuntza (language in general) with euskara (the Basque language).
Les noms de personne qui font une action: Nouns for people who perform an action are formed with -le, -tzaile, -ari or -gile depending on the word. You have to learn each word: ikasle (student), saltzaile (seller).
pilotari = joueur de pelote ; bertsolari: pilotari = pelota player; bertsolari = verse improviser; aizkolari = competitive wood-chopper.
-tegi forme un nom de lieu (où l'on fait: -tegi forms a place noun (where something is made or kept). After n or l it becomes -degi. Other place nouns use -etxe, -ola.
Après voyelle on garde -tegi : liburuteg: After a vowel we keep -tegi: liburutegi.
-dun signifie qui possède ; -tsu qui est: -dun means having; -tsu full of; -gabe without. They are found in many adjectives and nouns. -gabe can also be a separate word: diru gabe.
euskaldun veut dire qui possède le basqu: euskaldun means having Basque, i.e. a Basque speaker.
-ago exprime le comparatif, -en le super: -ago expresses the comparative, -en the superlative, -egi excess. The thing you compare to goes before baino (than). Equality is expressed with bezain.
Mikel est aussi grand qu'Ane: Mikel is as tall as Ane
Pour les courses : garesti = cher ; merk: For shopping: garesti = expensive; merkea = cheap.
Quelques adjectifs ont des comparatifs i: A few adjectives have irregular comparatives: on becomes hobe (better), asko becomes gehiago (more), gutxi becomes gutxiago (less). The superlative is hoberena.
In batua the comparative of on is hobe.
The irregular comparative of on is hobe.
Beaucoup d'adjectifs ont une forme adver: Many adjectives have a distinct adverb form: ona (good) becomes ondo or ongi (well); txarra (bad) becomes txarto or gaizki (badly); poliki means slowly. After a verb, you use the adverb.
Ne dites pas ona hitz egiten du : c'est: Don't say ona hitz egiten du: it's ondo.
Il parle bien basque : Euskaraz ___ hitz: He/She speaks Basque well: Euskaraz ___ hitz egiten du
-txo exprime le petit ou l'affection ; o: -txo expresses smallness or affection; you find it with family words. The terms amatxi and aitatxi mean grandmother and grandfather.
En batua standard grand-mère se dit amon: In standard batua, grandmother is amona and grandfather is aitona.
Quel suffixe donne un diminutif affectue: Which suffix gives an affectionate diminutive (amatxo)?
On forme des verbes avec -tu à partir d': You form verbs with -tu from adjectives and nouns (to become). After l or n, -tu becomes -du in writing.
Pour dire devenir + adjectif, on forme s: To say become + adjective, you often form a verb in -tu: handitu = to become big.
-kide désigne le compagnon dans une acti: -kide denotes a companion in an activity, -zale a fan or someone who loves something. These are very productive suffixes for naming people.
lankide est le terme courant pour collèg: lankide is the usual word for a work colleague.
Pour désigner un habitant, on ajoute -ta: To name an inhabitant, you add -tar to a place name after a consonant or a vowel other than i, and -ar after i. Place names keep their Basque form.
Habitant de Bilbao (forme de base, sans: Person from Bilbao (base form, without article):
Beaucoup de mots courants sont des compo: Many common words are compounds of two elements, sometimes adapted. The meaning can be worked out from the elements.
erdi (moitié, milieu) apparaît dans egue: erdi (half, middle) appears in eguerdi and gauerdi.
Le batua est la norme commune élaborée p: Batua is the common standard developed by Euskaltzaindia from 1968, mainly based on Gipuzkoan (gipuzkera) with contributions from other dialects. It is taught and written everywhere, while the dialects (bizkaiera, gipuzkera, nafarrera, lapurtera, zuberera...) remain spoken. As a learner, you need to learn batua and get used to local accents.

Dans la presse, l'administration et l'en: In the press, public administration and education, batua is used.
En bizkaiera, que dit-on à la place du b: In Bizkaian, what do people say instead of batua dut (I have, auxiliary)?
En bizkaiera on entend dot pour dut du b: In Bizkaian you hear dot for batua dut.
Euskal Herria est le Pays basque dans so: Euskal Herria is the Basque Country as a whole. Hegoalde (the south) includes the Basque Autonomous Community (Araba, Bizkaia, Gipuzkoa) and Navarre (Nafarroa). Iparralde (the north) includes Lapurdi, Nafarroa Beherea and Zuberoa, in France. In practice, Euskadi refers to the Basque Autonomous Community.
Vitoria est la capitale d'Araba: Vitoria is the capital of Araba
Pampelune est la capitale de Navarre: Pamplona is the capital of Navarre
Comment appelle-t-on la partie nord (fra: What is the northern (French) part of the Basque Country called?
Iparralde refers to the northern Basque Country.
Hegoalde is the south, the Spanish side.
Beaucoup de villes ont un nom officiel e: Many cities have an official Basque name that differs from the Spanish or French name. In Euskadi the road signs are often bilingual. In Valencia the Basque name is Valentzia.
Les deux formes sont comprises ; sur les: Both forms are understood; on road signs in Euskadi you see Donostia / San Sebastián.
Le nom basque de Bilbao est :: The Basque name of Bilbao is:
Bilbo is the Basque name of Bilbao.

De nombreux mots basques viennent du lat: Many Basque words come from Latin and look like French or Spanish. They help you memorise vocabulary, but their spelling is Basque.
Ne pas supposer qu'un mot ressemblant a: Don't assume a similar-looking word has the same meaning: check.
bake comes from Latin pax: peace.
Petits mots basques à ne pas confondre: Small Basque words not to be confused
Certains mots basques ressemblent à des: Some Basque words look like French words but mean something else. ez means no (not "is"), eta means and (not "summer"), bai means yes, ere means also, bat means one. ordu means hour or time.
Ne pas lire bai comme baie ni eta comme: Don't read bai as "bay" or eta as "summer".
Le basque inverse l'ordre français dans: Basque reverses the French order in almost every phrase: the adjective follows the noun (etxe handia), the possessor comes before the possessed (Mikelen etxea), the relative clause comes before the noun, the postposition follows its noun, and the verb comes last.
la maison de Mikel (litt. de Mikel la ma: Mikel's house (lit. of Mikel the house)
sur la table (litt. de la table sur): on the table (lit. of the table on)
Penser à l'ordre inverse : tout ce qui c: Think of the reversed order: everything that modifies comes before the word it modifies.
Un jeune garçon (mutil gazte) avec bat :: A young boy (mutil gazte) with bat:
Pas de vouvoiement obligatoire : zu, zue: No compulsory formal "you": zu, zuek, hi
Le pronom habituel est zu, même pour êtr: The usual pronoun is zu, even to be polite; it takes the singular verb (zara, duzu). zuek is the plural (zarete, duzue). The intimate hi exists but learners don't need to use it. There is no polite plural form: zuek is a true plural.
s'il vous plaît, quelle heure est-il ?: excuse me, what time is it?
zu verbe = singulier, même pour être pol: zu + verb = singular, even to be polite.
À une seule personne, par politesse, on: To one single person, to be polite, you say:
zu s'emploie pour une personne et se con: zu is used for one person and takes the singular verb.
zuek is the plural of zu.
euskaldun désigne celui qui parle basque: euskaldun refers to someone who speaks Basque, euskotar to someone who belongs to Euskal Herria (origin). A person who has adopted Basque is an euskaldun berri. erdara refers to any language other than Basque (Spanish on the southern side, French on the northern side).

Un habitant du Pays basque n'est pas for: A person living in the Basque Country isn't necessarily an euskaldun.
Les erreurs fréquentes sont : mettre un: Frequent mistakes are: putting a noun in the plural after a number (hiru etxeak), forgetting the ergative (Ni ikusi dut), using izan for age (naiz), placing the adjective before the noun, placing ez after the participle, saying joan behar naiz. Each point has its rule in the earlier lessons.
Se relire en vérifiant le nombre du nom,: Proofread by checking the number of the noun, the ergative and the position of the auxiliary.
